title: {{NAME}} and the Princess League of Impossible Goals
moral: When you use your gifts in service of something larger than yourself, those gifts grow beyond what you imagined possible.

pages.content:
The kingdom of Veldris had a football problem.

Not a bad football problem, exactly. More of a unnecessary-power-on-the-pitch problem, which was a subtler difficulty. The Veldris Princess League had always been the finest football league in the known kingdoms, but this season every single player on every team happened to also be a superhero, and the matches had become, by common agreement, somewhat unrealistic.

The most recent game had lasted four minutes before both goals had been scored simultaneously by players moving faster than the eye could follow, and the entire crowd had gone home confused.

{{NAME}} arrived in Veldris on a morning of pale winter sunshine, carrying the letter that had found him on his desk three days earlier. The letter was from Princess Damaris, captain of the Veldris Starfall squad, and it was terse, specific, and underlined in several places: needed, it read. Someone who cannot fly, cannot bend steel, cannot become invisible, and cannot redirect projectiles with their mind. Someone who simply knows how to play.

The training ground was a wide emerald pitch bordered by frost-white fences, and standing in its centre, watching three players run three separate laps simultaneously at completely unreasonable speeds, was Princess Damaris. She was tall, composed, and her crown, a simple circlet of blue steel, sat with the air of something that had never once slipped.

'You came,' she said. Not warmly, not coldly. Precisely.

pages.content:
The team was extraordinary and, underneath all the power, somewhat lost.

Mirca could fly, which she did at every opportunity, including during corner kicks, throw-ins, and once during a team huddle when she had hovered two metres above the group without apparently noticing.

Tabas could move at extraordinary speed, but had developed the habit of arriving at positions on the pitch several seconds before the ball did and then standing there in a state of athletic boredom while the rest of the game caught up.

'They're brilliant individually,' Princess Damaris said quietly to {{NAME}}, while the team practised at the far end. 'They have been brilliant individually for years. They have never quite managed to be brilliant together.'

{{NAME}} watched the practice. He could see it clearly, the way you see a puzzle once you know there is a puzzle: each player operating in their own orbit, their powers making individual excellence easy but collective play irrelevant. Why pass when you could do it yourself? Why track a run when you could simply be there?

'They've never needed each other,' he said.

'No.' Princess Damaris looked at him with frank assessment. 'But next week they face the Ironwood Eleven, and the Ironwood Eleven have no powers whatsoever. They play the most disciplined football I have ever seen. My team will be destroyed by people who trust each other, if nothing changes.'

{{NAME}} nodded slowly. 'Then we make them need each other,' he said.

pages.content:
The new training drills were, initially, deeply unpopular.

{{NAME}} designed them the night before on paper, working by lamplight, thinking of every game he had ever played in parks and schoolyards and the specific knowledge that passed between players who had learned to read each other. He could not make Mirca stop flying or make Tabas move at a normal pace. But he could build drills that made those powers useless unless the rest of the team had done their part first.

Mirca's aerial advantage meant nothing on crosses that never came because the passer had no support. Tabas's speed meant nothing in front of goal if the ball was never threaded to the right moment. One by one, in the brutal honesty of practice, each player arrived at the same realisation: the others were not obstacles in their individual excellence. They were the reason for it.

By the third day, Mirca was tracking runs she had never tracked before, curving down from altitude to meet passes that came at exactly the height she had learned to request. Tabas was arriving at positions not before the ball but with it, because someone had finally learned to find the space he'd be standing in.

Princess Damaris, who played every drill alongside her team, found spaces {{NAME}} had not designed for her, using instincts he hadn't taught but had simply made room for.

'There she is,' {{NAME}} murmured, watching the princess cut inside on the last drill of the day, collect, and slot home with the ease of someone who has always known where the goal is.

pages.content:
The match against the Ironwood Eleven was everything Damaris had predicted and nothing she had feared.

The Ironwood Eleven were disciplined and patient, pressing in coordinated waves, filling spaces the moment they opened, and they were not intimidated by superpowers in the way many teams were. They had played powered teams before, and they knew that individual brilliance, untethered, was easier to defend than simple passing.

But Veldris Starfall were not untethered. Not anymore.

For sixty minutes the match balanced on a knife's edge. Then Tabas received the ball in his own half, played a one-two with {{NAME}} that no speed-gifted player should ever take the time to do, and burst through a gap that the Ironwood midfield had left because they could not believe anyone would try something that required patience from someone with Tabas's pace.

'Now!' {{NAME}} called from the right wing, already making the run.

Tabas had never passed in that moment before. He always shot. Every game, for three seasons, he always shot.

He passed.

The ball arrived in exactly the place {{NAME}} was.

{{NAME}} struck it first time, clean and low, and the net moved with a sound like a quiet yes.

Mirca was there before the ball had stopped moving, arms around {{NAME}}, lifting him off the ground despite herself. Princess Damaris ran the length of the pitch to reach them, her blue-steel crown still perfectly level, her face completely unguarded for the first time.

pages.content:
They won two-nil. The second goal was Damaris, a header from a Mirca cross at the far post, which the princess took with the unhurried certainty of someone who knew the ball was coming and had all the time in the world to meet it.

The Ironwood Eleven applauded at the final whistle, which was the finest thing they could have done, and Veldris Starfall received it with the grace that comes from having been properly challenged.

The trophy ceremony was held on the pitch in the winter twilight, the frost-white fences catching the last gold of the afternoon.

Damaris addressed her team briefly and precisely, in the way she did everything. She thanked three people by name: Mirca, Tabas, and {{NAME}}. For Mirca and Tabas she cited what they had done differently. For {{NAME}} she paused, choosing the word carefully.

'For showing us,' she said, 'that what we already had was enough, if we could learn to use it together.'

{{NAME}} walked home under a sky full of cold quiet stars, his rose-gold cleats muffled on the frost.

He was warm and tired and good-tired, the kind that fills up from the inside rather than draining out.

He was almost asleep when a sharp knock at his window made him turn. A folded note had been slipped through the gap at the bottom.

Princess Damaris's handwriting. Two words and a question mark.

Next season?
